metadata.notes: Reference path for the Active Directory Domain-Admin → ransomware cascade, modelled on the Lynx intrusion (The DFIR Report, 'Cat's Got Your Files: Lynx Ransomware', 17 December 2025; intrusion of early March 2025; time to ransomware just under 178 hours across nine calendar days). Evidenced steps only. Shape: a variable prefix, the decisive compromise (a Tier-0 identity under attacker control, s3), and a near-invariant tail that is structurally #1 Abuse of Functions, with #7 wherever foreign executable content runs. Every cluster step records its own SRE (core §3.4). 'Decisive' marks where reach becomes domain-wide, not where loss of control begins. Attack path: … → #4 →[Δt=~minutes] #7 →[Δt=~minutes] #4 →[Δt=~minutes] #1 →[Δt=~minutes] #1 →[Δt=~minutes] #7 →[Δt=~5d] #4 →[Δt=~minutes] #1 →[Δt=~minutes] #7 →[Δt=~minutes] #1 →[Δt=~minutes] #1 + [DRE: C] →[Δt=~3d] #4 →[Δt=~minutes] #1 + [DRE: Av] →[Δt=~minutes] #1 →[Δt=~minutes] #7 + [DRE: Ac]. Compressions: the day-2 logons to hypervisors with the look-alike accounts (#1, since these accounts were self-enrolled; R-CRED) and the day-8 reconnaissance of domain controllers and Hyper-V hosts are omitted. Only session-opening logons are recorded, although every RDP hop with the stolen domain-admin credential is its own #4. The report does not mention credential dumping, shadow-copy deletion or log clearing, so none is recorded. Velocity is per transition: VC-3 (minutes) inside each session, VC-1 (days) between sessions. The ~10-minute beachhead→DC edge needs automated containment (DCS_c = TTC_P90/Δt < 1). Other prefix variants, as classified in the companion post: (B) Akira, Microsoft case study of 9 April 2025, no threat actor named: #4 [conf=low] VPN entry → … → #4 RDP to DC1 with a domain-admin credential → #1 recon → #1 GPO AV tampering → #1 two accounts created and added to Domain Admins → #1 logon as one of them. The encryption was blocked by attack disruption, so no #7/Ac is recorded (successes only). (C) Storm-2603, Cisco Talos 9 October 2025, incident of August 2025, moderate-confidence attribution, initial access not observed: #2 [conf=low] ToolShell → … → #1 admin accounts synced to Entra ID → #1 vSphere console → #1 GPO Defender off → #7 + [DRE: C] PowerShell exfil script → #7 + [DRE: Ac] fileless PowerShell encryptor / Warlock / Babuk on ESXi; Velociraptor 0.73.4.0 installs are #7, untimed. (D) Kerberoasting: #4 → #1 + [DRE: C] TGS requests → #4 cracked service account → #1 (ATT&CK T1558.003). (E) ZeroLogon CVE-2020-1472: #2 + [DRE: I] machine-account password reset → #4 logon as the DC account → #1 + [DRE: C] DCSync. Sources: DFIR Report (Lynx); Microsoft Security Blog 'How cyberattackers exploit domain controllers using ransomware' (9 April 2025; >78% of human-operated cyberattacks breach a DC, DC is the primary spreader in >35%); Cisco Talos 'Velociraptor leveraged in ransomware attacks' (9 October 2025); CISA AA24-109A (Akira, updated 13 November 2025); Secura Zerologon whitepaper (2020). Companion analysis: https://www.tlctc.net/ad-ransomware-tlctc-cascade.html (The #1-Cascade). Revision 2026-10-25: rebuilt as an evidence-only Lynx path. The earlier composite carried an actor label ('Storm-0300') that Microsoft's case study does not support. It also had an exfiltration #7 that Lynx does not evidence (the upload went through a browser), DCSync, shadow-copy and log-clearing steps that Lynx does not document, a non-registry boundary context, per-incident velocity classes, and ZeroLogon's [DRE: C] on the exploit step. Classified against the v2.6 dictionary; v2.7 is classification-preserving.

path_sequence.notes: Acquisition of the two domain credentials used in s1 and s3. The DFIR Report found no brute force, no spraying, no on-host privilege escalation and no credential dumping. It assesses that both credentials were compromised before the intrusion: infostealer logs, reuse from a breach, or an initial-access broker. No acquisition telemetry survived on the target estate, so no cluster can be defended (R-UNRES-8, R-UNRES-9). Each candidate route would be its own chain, for example #9 → #7 + [DRE: C] for a stealer infection.

Day 1. Successful RDP logon to an internet-exposed beachhead host with valid credentials and an elevated token. No failed authentications precede it, which is the forensic signature of pre-acquired credentials. Credential application is #4 (R-CRED, Axiom X).

SoftPerfect Network Scanner (netscan.exe 7.2.7, with config and license file) dropped onto the beachhead desktop over the RDP session and run against the internal range, with share write checks. A legitimate product brought in by the attacker is a foreign-introduced tool, so its execution is #7 (R-EXEC). Native discovery commands run in the same session (ipconfig, route print, systeminfo) are designed functions and are not recorded separately.

About ten minutes after the first logon, RDP from the beachhead to a domain controller with a DIFFERENT domain-admin account, also compromised beforehand. This is the decisive compromise, where a Tier-0 identity is under attacker control and reach becomes domain-wide. It is one SRE among many, since every cluster step records its own. Credential application is #4.

Accounts 'administratr' and a look-alike of an existing user are created with dsa.msc and set to never expire. A third look-alike is created on day 1 or day 2; the report is inconsistent on this. The enrolment function is used outside any grant, so this is #1 (R-SCOPE, R-CRED). Because the directory issued these identities to the attacker, later logons with them claim no one else's identity and are NOT #4 (R-CRED, self-issued identity). The day-2 hypervisor logons with them are #1. Axiom IV: the typosquat naming is a tell, not a classification input.

'administratr' and the first look-alike are added to Domain Admins, and 'administratr' also to Group Policy Creator Owners. The third account goes into a domain-specific privileged group. These are designed group-membership functions used outside any grant.

AnyDesk installed as a service on the domain controller, then never used. The installer and service are foreign-introduced code executing (R-EXEC). The step succeeded as persistence, so it is recorded even though the channel stayed idle. Day 1 ends with a registry query for hypervisor hostnames.
Day 6. RDP back to the beachhead from the same source IP and workstation name. Re-applying a stolen credential is #4 each time.
NetExec (nxc.exe) downloaded through Microsoft Edge. Ingress transfer uses a designed client function and moves a file without running it, so it is #1 (ATT&CK T1105 mapping). R-EXEC fires at s9.

NetExec run for about two minutes against the /24 over SMB (445) with domain-admin credentials. The report's detail section describes live-host enumeration; its summary calls it a password spray. Either way the attacker-introduced tool executes, so this is #7 (R-EXEC). The SMB authentications it makes with the stolen credential are folded into this step.

File shares on two file servers browsed and archived with 7-Zip's Explorer 'Add to archive' (7zG.exe), with the archives saved to the desktop. These are designed file-access and archive functions (ATT&CK T1560.001 → #1). The report does not say whether 7-Zip was already installed. The disclosure is recorded at s11, where the data leaves the organization's control.

The archives are uploaded one by one to the temporary file-sharing service temp.sh; browser history shows its /upload URI. A browser's upload form is a designed client function and no attacker code runs, so this is #1 + [DRE: C]. The April 2026 edition recorded a #7 'exfil tool' here, which Lynx does not evidence. Contrast Storm-2603 (Talos), where a PowerShell script did the upload: #7 + [DRE: C].

Day 9. RDP to the beachhead from a new source IP (a day-8 session from the same IP did the reconnaissance omitted here), then RDP to a backup server with the stolen domain-admin credential. #4 at each authentication.
evidence_refs: Event 4624 logon type 10 on beachhead and backup server

path_sequence.notes: In the Veeam Backup & Replication console, backup jobs are deleted and backups are removed from the configuration database. This is a designed administrative function used outside any grant. [DRE: Av]: the backup data is gone, not merely unusable. Contrast: the backup administrator doing the same inside their grant would be Abuse of Rights (no cluster, no SRE, the chain starts at the DRE), with an identical log entry.

The Lynx payload w.exe is copied to the desktop of the compromised domain-admin account, and on one server to the root of E:. A designed file-copy function moves a file without running it, so this is #1. The run is s15.

w.exe is run manually via cmd (e.g. --dir E:\ --mode fast --verbose --noprint) on several backup and file servers, each reached over RDP. Foreign executable content runs, so this is #7 with fec_executed (R-EXEC). [DRE: Ac]: the data is present but unusable. Axiom III: 'ransomware' is the outcome label, not a cluster. This one step stands for the per-host s14 → s15 pair repeated on each server, and a forensic record would enumerate each pair.
